source: RangDale9 ch2, ch8; KDT8 ch4-5, ch8, ch30; GG14 ch3, ch9; Ghosh FEP, Medhi PMECP, Sarkar OCR, Bennett, Golan, GG14 p324

cards.front: Define bioassay and explain why a standard is run alongside the unknown.
cards.back: Bioassay measures the potency of a drug or unknown mediator from the size of the biological effect it produces. The unknown (U) is compared with a standard (S) on the same test system, because absolute 'units' (e.g. pigeon or mouse units) differ between laboratories, whereas the relative potency of U and S can be agreed. The assay estimates the dose of U that gives the same effect as a known dose of S.

cards.front: What is a 2 + 2 (parallel-line) bioassay, and why is it used?
cards.back: The minimal parallel-line design: two doses of standard (S1, S2) and two of unknown (U1, U2), chosen to fall on the linear part of the log dose-response curve. Doses are given repeatedly in random order, which measures the variability of the test system and lets the confidence limits of the potency ratio be calculated. Example: a modified 2 + 2 assay in patients showed morphine to be about 13 times as potent an analgesic as codeine.

cards.front: Parallel-line assay: how is potency read?
cards.text: In a parallel-line assay the potency ratio is read from the {{horizontal distance}} between the standard and unknown log dose-response lines. A simple ratio is invalid if the lines are not {{parallel}} or the maximal responses differ.

cards.front: Short note: Requirements of a valid bioassay

points: Compare unknown with a standard on the same preparation
Compare equi-effective doses from dose-response curves, not responses to equal doses
Log dose-response lines of standard and unknown must be parallel
Maximal responses must be similar; differing mechanisms or a partial agonist invalidate a simple potency ratio
Biological variation is the main problem
Minimise variation, avoid systematic error, and estimate limits of error
Randomised order of doses; observer (and subject) unaware of the dose
Graded or quantal responses need different statistics

cards.front: In a bioassay, what goes wrong if the log dose-response lines of standard and unknown are not parallel?
cards.back: The potency ratio is no longer a single number: the unknown is not behaving like a dilution of the standard, so it may act by a different mechanism or be a partial agonist with a lower maximum. Equi-effective doses are compared from dose-response curves, which only works when the lines are parallel and the maxima similar.

cards.front: Case: you must estimate histamine in an unknown extract using an isolated tissue. Outline a valid design.
cards.back: Use a standard histamine-sensitive preparation such as guinea pig ileum (H1 contraction). Run the standard and the unknown on the same tissue, compare equi-effective doses from dose-response curves, and check the log dose-response lines are parallel with similar maxima. Randomise the order of doses and keep the observer unaware of dose to limit error, since biological variation is the main problem. Express the result as potency relative to the standard.

cards.front: Graded vs quantal dose-response: how do they differ?
cards.back: Graded responses are continuous (e.g. fall in BP, strength of contraction) and are measured in each individual, giving a sigmoidal curve of response against log dose. Quantal responses are all-or-none (e.g. death, convulsion). The proportion of a population responding is plotted against dose, giving a cumulative curve from which median doses (ED50, LD50) are read.

cards.front: Define ED50, TD50 and LD50.
cards.back: ED50: the dose producing the specified therapeutic effect in 50% of subjects. TD50: the dose producing a defined toxic effect in 50% of subjects. LD50: the dose that kills 50% of the test animals.

cards.front: Potency vs efficacy: define each and give one example.
cards.back: Potency is the dose or concentration needed for a given effect (its position on the dose axis). Efficacy is the maximal effect a drug can produce (the height of the plateau). Morphine is more efficacious than aspirin as an analgesic; pethidine is less potent than morphine but equally efficacious.

cards.front: Therapeutic index formulae
cards.text: Therapeutic index in animals = {{LD50}} / {{ED50}}. In humans the index uses {{TD50}} in place of LD50, because TD50 is the dose producing a defined toxic effect in 50% of people.

cards.front: What is the dose ratio, and how does a Schild plot measure competitive antagonist affinity?
cards.back: Dose ratio (r): the factor by which agonist concentration must be raised in the presence of an antagonist to restore a given response. With a reversible competitive antagonist the log concentration-effect curve shifts right without change in slope or maximum, and r increases linearly with antagonist concentration. A Schild plot of log(r - 1) against log antagonist concentration gives the antagonist's equilibrium dissociation constant (KB) from the abscissal intercept, e.g. propranolol on isolated guinea-pig atria. Antagonist affinity measured this way is used to classify receptors.

cards.front: Short note: Therapeutic index and margin of safety

points: Gap between therapeutic and adverse-effect dose-response curves = safety margin or therapeutic index
Animals: TI = LD50 / ED50
Humans: TI = TD50 / ED50
Measurable only in animals (LD50 form)
LD50 does not reflect adverse effects at therapeutic doses
ED50 depends on the effect chosen (aspirin for headache vs as antirheumatic)
Individual variation in efficacy and toxicity is not captured
Clinically the therapeutic window (minimal therapeutic dose to maximal acceptable dose) is more relevant
Narrow-margin drugs need individualised dosing and monitoring

cards.front: Why is the LD50/ED50 therapeutic index a poor guide to safety, and what is used clinically instead?
cards.back: LD50 is measurable only in animals and ignores adverse effects at therapeutic doses; ED50 changes with the effect chosen (e.g. aspirin for headache versus as antirheumatic), and individual variation is not captured. In humans TD50/ED50 is the analogous index, but clinically the therapeutic window (minimal therapeutic dose to maximal acceptable dose) matters more, and narrow-margin drugs need individualised dosing and monitoring.

cards.front: Frog rectus abdominis: what phenomenon does it demonstrate?
cards.back: Repeated or high doses of acetylcholine produce progressively smaller contractions; shortly after a high (100-fold) dose the response is markedly reduced and returns only after time is allowed. This illustrates receptor desensitisation at the nicotinic end plate. The preparation is also a classical system for studying acetylcholine responses at nicotinic receptors.

cards.front: Classify: isolated tissues and what each tests
cards.text: Guinea pig ileum is used to show {{muscarinic}} actions of acetylcholine blocked by atropine, and its contraction is a standard bioassay for {{histamine}} (H1). Frog rectus abdominis shows {{nicotinic}} end-plate desensitisation. Isolated guinea pig {{atria}} are used to measure competitive antagonism of isoprenaline by propranolol.

cards.front: Which isolated tissue shows muscarinic ACh contraction blocked by atropine and also serves as a histamine bioassay?
cards.back: Guinea pig ileum. ACh contracts it through muscarinic receptors (atropine blocks this), and its H1-mediated contraction gives a standard bioassay for histamine.

cards.front: Isolated guinea pig atria: which drug pair is classically studied, and what is learned?
cards.back: Isoprenaline with the antagonist propranolol. The atria show competitive antagonism: the isoprenaline curve shifts right in parallel, which lets the antagonist affinity be measured and receptors classified.

cards.front: Short note: Isolated organ bath preparations

points: A strip of smooth muscle or other tissue is held in an organ bath, and contraction or relaxation is recorded
Response is plotted against concentration as a concentration-effect curve
Estimate maximal response and potency of agonists
Detect specific activity early in screening (e.g. antihistaminic, vasodilator)
Measure antagonist affinity by dose ratio and Schild analysis
The classical technique of pharmacology, still widely used alongside molecular and cellular assays

cards.front: Short note: Isometric force recording in isolated tissues

points: Tissue is held at a fixed length, so contraction appears as force
Force is recorded by a transducer and drawn on a polygraph
Strip or ring mounted in a small organ bath of physiological salt solution (e.g. Krebs bicarbonate)
One end fixed to the bath, the other to a strain gauge or force-displacement transducer
Resting tension applied, e.g. 2 g for spiral strips of bovine coronary artery in a 4 mL bath
Test relaxant or contractile drugs against standard agonists
Rabbit aorta rings contracted by KCl or noradrenaline show calcium-channel antagonism as relaxation
Isolated heart: contractile force measured isometrically by a force transducer

cards.front: Short note: Human tissue assays in clinical development

points: Early human study with limited exposure and no therapeutic intent, to decide go or no-go
Aims: refine and validate a biomarker assay and test drug effect on its target in human tissue
Gives human PK-PD data and checks that the mechanism seen in animals occurs in humans
In vitro pyrogen test using donated human blood
Human skin from surgery or donated cadavers used for penetration studies
US National Disease Research Interchange supplies human tissue to researchers
Human blood monocytes incubated with a glucocorticoid; receptor expression measured by FACS
Pre-clinical safety data required for phase 0 are small, so fewer animal studies are needed

cards.front: Case: design an organ-bath experiment to prove propranolol is a competitive antagonist of isoprenaline and estimate its affinity.
cards.back: Record isoprenaline concentration-effect curves on guinea pig atria alone, then with increasing propranolol concentrations. Competitive antagonism shows as parallel rightward shifts with unchanged maximum. Calculate the dose ratio (r) at each antagonist concentration, plot log(r - 1) against log antagonist concentration (Schild plot), and read the equilibrium dissociation constant KB from the abscissal intercept.

cards.front: Rat paw oedema: what does it screen, and what are its limits?
cards.back: Irritant chemicals injected into a rat's paw make it swollen and tender. Drugs that reduce this swelling predict well the symptomatic relief of inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, so it is used to screen anti-inflammatory drugs. Limit: such simple models predict efficacy only with fair accuracy and are far from perfect.

cards.front: MES vs PTZ anticonvulsant screens: what does each predict?
cards.back: MES: a brief high-intensity shock to the rodent head gives tonic flexion, tonic extension and clonic convulsions. Drugs that abolish the tonic (extensor) phase (e.g. phenytoin, carbamazepine) are effective in GTCS and complex partial seizures; activity reflects action on seizure spread. PTZ: injection produces clonic seizures, prevented by drugs effective in absence and myoclonic seizures (e.g. ethosuximide, valproate, clonazepam); activity reflects action on the seizure focus. Other models: chronic focal seizures (alumina cream on monkey cortex) and kindling.

cards.front: What makes a good animal model of human disease?
cards.back: It should resemble the human disease in pathophysiological phenotype (face validity), causation (construct validity) and response to treatment (predictive validity). Difficulties: many psychiatric diseases cannot be observed in animals; causes of degenerative diseases are complex; selecting models by response to known drugs may miss new mechanisms; transgenic models can mislead (cystic fibrosis gene defect affects mainly the intestine in mice).

cards.front: Classify: animal models of human disease used in drug screening
cards.text: Examples include {{kindled}} seizures in rats, {{spontaneously hypertensive}} rats (genetic model), experimental tuberculosis in mice, and {{alloxan}}-induced diabetes in rats or dogs.

cards.front: Animal models of depression: principle and limitations.
cards.back: Mild stress procedures, such as the forced swim test or inescapable foot shock, produce behavioural states (social withdrawal, loss of appetite, reduced motor activity) that mimic aspects of human depression and are used to test antidepressants. Limitation: no known animal condition corresponds to inherited human depression, and no clear brain pathology is defined, so face and construct validity are poor; models selected on response to known drugs may miss new mechanisms.

cards.front: Short note: Role of the mouse as an experimental animal

points: Rodents, including mice, are used first; larger animals follow
Unfavourable compounds are dropped at each stage, so few reach human trials
Transgenic mice carry an introduced gene (knock-in) or an inactivated gene (knockout)
Used to build disease models for drug testing
Rodents preferred for genetic toxicity tests, e.g. mouse-specific locus test and micronucleus test
Rodents preferred for embryotoxicity and reproductive toxicity studies
Mouse local lymph node assay: test substance applied to mouse ear for three days
Lymph node cell proliferation measured; accepted by EPA, OECD and FDA as preferred assay
Mice immunised to raise antibody-producing cells for monoclonal antibody production
Behaviour tests such as tail suspension and rota-rod

cards.front: Short note: Animal models for testing learning and memory

points: Morris water maze: hidden platform in a circular pool; escape latency recorded over at least 5 days
Probe test 24 h after training, with platform removed, measures spatial memory
Y-maze, T-maze, radial arm maze and Barnes circular maze
Inhibitory (passive) avoidance uses negative reinforcement to test long-term memory
Step-through and step-down variants
Scopolamine (muscarinic antagonist) impairs learning and memory in rodents and humans
Dizocilpine (NMDA antagonist) produces memory impairment for testing memory enhancers

cards.front: Short note: Guinea pig as an experimental animal

points: Ileum: acetylcholine contraction blocked by atropine, histamine response unaffected
Ileum contraction is a standard bioassay for histamine
Atria: competitive antagonism of isoprenaline by propranolol
Guinea pigs are the most sensitive common species to histamine
Histamine-induced bronchoconstriction is strong; anaphylactic bronchoconstriction is largely prevented by antihistamines
Draize eye and skin irritancy tests use rabbits and guinea pigs
Guinea pig maximisation test used for skin sensitisation
Armstrong/Harber test in guinea pig when a drug or metabolite may cause photosensitivity

cards.front: Short note: Animal models in vaccine development and testing

points: Preclinical stage: in vitro work, then in vivo testing in animals, before any human dosing
Follows the exploratory stage, where candidate antigens are identified and may be modified by recombinant DNA technology
Immunogenicity: the immune response the vaccine provokes
Safety and toxicity
Approximate dose range and suitable formulation
Non-human primates (monkeys): the oral polio vaccine was first tested here for adverse effects and immunogenicity
Transgenic animals are now used in preclinical protocols for more accurate prediction of human reactions
Satisfactory preclinical data lead to phase I, the first human study in a small group (about 20) of healthy adults

cards.front: Short note: Screening a new molecule for anti-anxiety activity

points: Rodents avoid brightly lit or open spaces, so anxiolytics change their exploration and avoidance
Test drug given about 30 min before testing (i.p. in the plus-maze protocol)
Elevated plus maze (Pellow, 1985): anxiolytic effect is more time and entries in the open arms
Light-dark (black and white) box: anxiolytics increase crossings between the chambers
Social interaction test: anxiolytics reverse the suppression of social contact in a bright, unfamiliar setting
Geller-Seifter operant conflict test: high predictive value for classical anxiolytics
Vogel lick-conflict test: anxiolytics increase the number of shocks accepted while drinking
Diazepam increases time spent in the open arms of the elevated plus maze

cards.front: Short note: Transgenic animals

points: Animal carrying a foreign gene, or an altered gene, deliberately placed in its genome
The new gene is inherited by offspring in the same way as native genes
Mice are the usual species: over 80% of mouse genes work like human genes, and they breed quickly
DNA microinjection into the male pronucleus of a fertilised ovum: first effective method in mammals; insertion is random
Embryonic stem cell transfer: targeted by homologous recombination; the method of choice for knockout animals
Retrovirus-mediated transfer into an early embryo, which is then implanted
Disease models: mice carrying the human poliovirus receptor can be infected; APP transgenic mice model Alzheimer disease
Toxicology test animals, drug efficacy testing, production of pharmaceutical proteins, and veterinary uses such as higher milk yield
Insertional mutation can disrupt important biological processes
Unregulated gene expression and side effects such as arthritis, dermatitis or cancer
Animal welfare and ethical objections

cards.front: Essay: Preclinical pharmacological screening of a new analgesic and anti-inflammatory drug

points: Animal tests expose the whole pharmacological profile before human use
Rodent first, then a larger animal; unfavourable compounds are rejected at each step
Simple rapid screening tests for the sought activity (e.g. analgesic activity)
Isolated organ tests for specific activities
Rat paw oedema from irritant chemicals predicts anti-inflammatory benefit
Models need face, construct and predictive validity
Detailed confirmatory tests; related activities such as antipyretic and anti-inflammatory action of an analgesic
Systemic pharmacology on major organ systems; mechanism of action
Dose-response relationship, maximal effect, potency and efficacy compared with existing drugs
Pharmacokinetics, then toxicity testing
Animal efficacy may not translate (e.g. substance P antagonists were analgesic in animals but inactive in humans)

cards.front: Acute toxicity study: design and endpoint.
cards.back: Single escalating doses are given to small groups of animals (usually two species, two routes) and observed for overt effects and mortality for 1 to 3 days. Goals: the no-effect dose, the maximum tolerated dose and, where needed, the LD50, now estimated with the smallest possible number of animals. Organ toxicity is examined by histopathology.

cards.front: Subacute and chronic toxicity studies: duration and parameters.
cards.back: Subacute (subchronic): repeated doses for about 2 to 12 weeks (Katzung: 2 weeks to 3 months), usually three doses in two species; the longer the intended human use, the longer the test. Doses are chosen from ED50 and LD50. Chronic: a rodent and at least one non-rodent for 6 to 12 months, required when the drug will be used long term, and usually run alongside early clinical trials. Both record overt effects, food intake, body weight, haematology, biochemistry and organ histopathology.

cards.front: How is the LD50 estimated from acute toxicity data?
cards.back: Two calculation methods. Graphical (Miller and Tainter): convert each group's percentage mortality to a probit, plot probit against log dose after correcting the 0% and 100% groups, and read the dose at 50% mortality. Arithmetical (Karber): no plotting; uses the mean number dead in each dose interval and the dose difference between groups.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p160
Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p162

cards.front: Classify: species and routes in toxicity testing
cards.text: Toxicity testing uses at least {{two}} species, one {{rodent}} and one {{non-rodent}}, dosed by the {{oral}} and {{parenteral}} routes.

cards.front: Short note: Preclinical toxicity studies

points: At least two species, one rodent and one non-rodent, by oral and parenteral routes
Acute, subacute and chronic studies
Effects on spermatogenesis, ovulation, fertility, mating, parturition and the developing foetus (teratogenicity)
Two species, usually one rodent and rabbits
Carcinogenicity: dosing for 2 years or the whole life of the animal, required for drugs used long term
Mutagenicity: bacteria (Ames test), mammalian cells and intact rodents
Conducted under Good Laboratory Practice (GLP)
Thalidomide disaster led to more extensive teratogenicity testing

cards.front: Short note: Genotoxicity testing

points: Ames test: detects mutations in bacteria
Mutations and genetic stability in mammalian cells in culture
Intact rodents: dominant lethal test and clastogenicity (chromosome damage) in mice
Part of the preclinical safety package with carcinogenicity testing
Rare effects may still be missed for statistical reasons

cards.front: Graphical versus Karber method for LD50: which to choose and why?
cards.back: Graphical method is simple and accurate in most cases and should be tried first, but needs probit plotting. Karber's method needs no plot and is the simplest and quickest, though crude, so it suits small animal numbers. Ghosh's crotalabumine example gave 79.5 mg/kg graphically and 81 mg/kg by Karber, so the two agree closely.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p160
Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p162

cards.front: Essay: Preclinical safety evaluation of a new drug candidate

points: Aim: identify likely human toxicities and those to monitor in trials
Two species, two routes
No-effect dose, maximum tolerated dose, LD50 if needed
Subacute and chronic designs with haematology, biochemistry and histopathology
Reproduction and teratogenicity
Mutagenicity (Ames, mammalian cells, rodents)
Carcinogenicity where long-term use is planned
First human dose usually 1/100 to 1/10 of the no-effect (non-toxic) dose in animals
Time-consuming and expensive (2 to 6 years)
Large numbers of animals
Extrapolation to humans imperfect; rare effects missed
GLP-compliant data package before human trials

cards.front: How is the use of animals in preclinical testing being reduced?
cards.text: Progress has been made in {{reducing the number}} of animals needed while keeping data valid; {{cell and tissue culture}} in vitro methods and {{computer modelling}} are increasingly used, though their {{predictive value}} is still limited.

cards.front: What is CPCSEA, and what are its functions?
cards.back: The Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals: a statutory body under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, formed in 1964 and revived in 1998. Sarkar lists its member secretary under the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying. Functions: register establishments that experiment on or breed animals; appoint nominees to Institutional Animal Ethics Committees (IAECs); approve animal house facilities after inspection; permit experiments on animals; recommend import of animals; act against violations; and train nominees.

cards.front: Short note: The 3Rs and the 4th R in animal experimentation

points: Russell and Burch defined alternatives as the three Rs: Replacement, Reduction, Refinement
CPCSEA introduced the 3Rs in India in 1999 and adopted a 4th R, Rehabilitation, in 2006 (others use Responsibility)
Absolute: no animals (human cells, computer models, dummies); relative: animal cells or tissues
Using lower organisms (microorganisms, invertebrates, eggs) instead of higher animals
Fewer animals where use is essential: better skills, pilot studies, proper design and statistics
Modify methods to minimise pain and distress; define humane endpoints
After-care of experimental animals until natural death; aseptic procedures; one major procedure per animal; proper post-operative care

cards.front: Short note: Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC)

points: Every animal study (including tissue or cell collection from animals) must be approved by the IAEC first
Constituted in every CPCSEA-registered laboratory; CPCSEA guidelines govern animal maintenance
Held at scheduled intervals, with expedited review if needed
Decisions by consensus; dissent minuted; unresolved cases referred to CPCSEA
Multiple surgical procedures on one animal only if specified in the protocol and approved by the IAEC
Knows CPCSEA guidelines and the 4Rs; reviews proposals for humane issues and animal numbers
Visits the animal house at least once a year and submits an inspection report
Informs CPCSEA if no meetings are held for 6 months

cards.front: If alternatives to animals are improving, why does safety testing in two species remain required?
cards.back: In vitro cell and tissue methods and computer models reduce animal numbers, but their predictive value is still limited; many effects, especially rare ones, are only seen in whole animals, and animal-to-human extrapolation is imperfect. So two-species safety testing is still done before human trials, while reduction, refinement and replacement are pursued.

cards.front: Essay: Use of animals in pharmacological research: value, limits and alternatives

points: Animal studies expose the pharmacological and toxicological profile before human use
Simple models often predict human efficacy (ferret motion-sickness model, rat paw oedema)
Safety testing in two species is required before trials
Many human diseases have no animal counterpart
Validity (face, construct, predictive) often incomplete
Animal-to-human extrapolation imperfect; rare effects missed; large numbers of animals
Isolated organ, cell and tissue culture methods
Computer modelling
Human microdosing (phase 0) studies give early human PK
Reduce animal numbers while keeping data valid; Good Laboratory Practice standards

cards.front: Which salt solutions contain no magnesium or phosphate ions?
cards.back: De Jalon, Frog-Ringer and Ringer-Locke (Medhi). Ghosh names Ringer, Frog-Ringer and De Jalon.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p9

cards.front: Which gas aerates each common PSS?
cards.back: Air: Tyrode and Frog-Ringer. Oxygen alone: Ringer-Locke. 95% O2 + 5% CO2: Krebs, De Jalon and McEwen.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p11

cards.front: Why is CaCl2 added last when making a PSS?
cards.back: Calcium with bicarbonate precipitates and makes the solution turbid. Medhi says add CaCl2 last; Ghosh says add the bicarbonate only at set-up.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p8

cards.front: How long may a prepared PSS be kept?
cards.back: Prepare it fresh. Medhi allows up to 24 h in a fridge; longer storage invites microbial growth from glucose. Ghosh says prepare fresh on the day of the experiment.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p8

cards.front: What is the maximum acceptable error when preparing a PSS?
cards.back: 1%. Hygroscopic CaCl2 and MgCl2 are best added from stock solution.

cards.front: How do you weigh a hydrated salt in place of an anhydrous one?
cards.back: Scale the weight by the molar mass ratio: 0.2 g anhydrous CaCl2 needs 0.26 g CaCl2.2H2O (147/111).
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p8

cards.front: Which non-hygroscopic magnesium salt replaces MgCl2 in a PSS?
cards.back: MgSO4. MgCl2 is hygroscopic and hard to weigh; the sulphate ion has no harmful effect.

cards.front: De Jalon solution: how does it differ from Ringer-Locke?
cards.back: Same salts as Ringer-Locke, but one-quarter the CaCl2 and half the glucose. Medhi's table also gives bicarbonate 5 g vs 2 g per 10 L, which Ghosh does not mention.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p9

cards.front: Which PSS suits non-innervated muscle, and which suits nerve-muscle preparations?
cards.back: Tyrode for non-innervated muscle; Krebs for nerve-muscle preparations. Krebs may be used for any tissue.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p11

cards.front: Why is carbogen, not pure oxygen, used with a bicarbonate PSS?
cards.back: Pure O2 drives off CO2 from the bicarbonate buffer, so the PSS becomes alkaline. Adding 5% CO2 prevents this.

cards.front: What pH range should a PSS be kept in, and what does a low pH do?
cards.back: pH 7.3 to 7.4. At lower pH the tonus of the tissue tends to fall, altering drug effects.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p8

cards.front: What happens to isolated intestine when the bath is cooled below 37 C?
cards.back: Tonus rises, contractions become smaller, and contraction and relaxation times increase.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p8

cards.front: Histamine stock 1 mg/mL: 0.2 mL added to a 10 mL bath gives what final concentration?
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p11

cards.front: First human dose from acute animal toxicity data: what rule do rat and dog tests give?
cards.back: Start from the minimum effective dose in the acute test. Rat test: one two-hundredth as the single starting dose; dog test: one-tenth. Same route.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p160

cards.front: Short note: Biostandardization

points: Biological standardisation is a specialised bioassay
Potency of material of unknown strength is compared with a standard of the same substance
Vaccines and sera are biologicals that are standardised by bioassay
Potency is therefore expressed in units, not by weight
Unfractionated heparin: 1 unit stops clotting of 1 mL citrated sheep plasma for 1 hour after 0.2 mL of 1% CaCl2
Heparin varies in molecular size, so only bioassay standardises it
Such biologicals are standardised by bioassay and need cold storage to keep potency

cards.front: Define biological standardisation.
cards.back: Bioassay of a material of unknown potency against a standard preparation of the same substance, so potency is stated relative to that standard.

cards.front: How is one unit of unfractionated heparin defined?
cards.back: The amount that stops 1 mL of citrated sheep plasma from clotting for 1 hour after 0.2 mL of 1% CaCl2 is added. Because its molecular size varies, it is standardised only by bioassay.

cards.front: Short note: Merits and demerits of screening methods for antidiabetic and antihypertensive activity

points: Alloxan or streptozotocin in rats or dogs: quick hyperglycaemia, but a type I model only
Neonatal STZ rat: hyperglycaemia resembling type II diabetes
Genetic obese models (ob/ob, KK, OLETF): spontaneous diabetes with obesity
In vitro enzyme and tissue assays (alpha-glucosidase, insulin secretion, glucose uptake): simple, but no whole-animal effect
SHR: hypertension with complications of hypertension, a disease-like model
SHR may not match essential hypertension because renal sodium handling differs
Drug-induced models (cholinomimetic, angiotensin II, L-NAME) probe specific mechanisms
Tail-cuff method: non-invasive and repeatable in conscious rats
Direct arterial recording in anaesthetised animals: precise but invasive and terminal

cards.front: Why does stratifying animals reduce sampling error?
cards.back: Animals are grouped into strata of similar individuals (same litter, sex, age or body weight), so less variable groups are compared. Other ways to cut sampling error: more subjects, paired samples and sufficient dose.

cards.front: What do 95% fiducial limits of a mean tell you?
cards.back: The range in which the population mean lies in 95% of cases. It is the sample mean plus or minus t(0.05) times the standard error, with N minus 1 degrees of freedom.

cards.front: Short note: Fiducial limits in bioassay

points: Confidence (fiducial) limits: bounds for the population mean from a sample
Only 5% of samples would give a mean outside these limits by chance
m = x plus or minus t(0.05) x standard error
t is read from the t table at N minus 1 degrees of freedom
Potencies are compared on the log scale; geometric means and their limits are used
Index of precision (variance divided by regression coefficient): 0.05 or less is excellent, 0.1 to 0.2 acceptable

cards.front: What does ANOVA separate?
cards.back: Total variation into variation between groups (due to treatment) and variation within groups (random error). A large between-group part relative to within-group error points to a real treatment effect.

cards.front: Why use the coefficient of variation instead of the standard deviation?
cards.back: When two samples have widely different means, the standard deviation alone cannot say which is more variable. The coefficient of variation expresses variability relative to the mean, so the two can be compared.

cards.front: Index of precision in a bioassay: what do the values mean?
cards.back: Index of precision is the variance divided by the regression coefficient. Values of 0.05 or less are excellent, 0.1 to 0.2 are acceptable, and 0.5 or more are unacceptable.

cards.front: Short note: Acetylcholine detection and estimation

points: Parallel assays on guinea pig ileum, rabbit tissues or blood pressure of anaesthetised cat or rat give muscarinic action blocked by atropine
Frog rectus abdominis and leech muscle give nicotinic action blocked by curare
Eserine potentiates the response in all these preparations
Activity is destroyed by boiling with NaOH, but not by weak acid
Blood cholinesterase destroys ACh quickly; eserine slows this
Bath fluid contains mepyramine, hexamethonium and morphine to block other receptors

cards.front: Which tissue shows nicotinic acetylcholine action and what blocks it?
cards.back: Frog rectus abdominis (and leech dorsal muscle). Curare blocks the response; eserine potentiates it.

cards.front: What does blood do to an acetylcholine solution, and how is that slowed?
cards.back: Blood cholinesterase destroys acetylcholine, so activity falls quickly. Eserine (an anticholinesterase) slows this loss.

cards.front: Short note: In vitro evaluation of anticancer drugs

points: Cancer cell lines grown in microtitre plates; growth measured by colour proportional to cell number
Compare proliferation with and without the drug after a fixed time
Test normal cell lines alongside cancer lines
Clinical promise needs selectivity of at least two orders of magnitude
Two identical sets are exposed; one is assayed, the other is re-incubated in fresh medium
MTT and XTT tetrazolium reduction assays; cell lines from national repositories, e.g. NCCS Pune
National Cancer Institute runs screens on 60 cancer cell lines
Ehrlich ascites carcinoma in mice: median survival time and viable tumour cell count

cards.front: What does an MTT assay measure?
cards.back: Metabolic reduction of a tetrazolium dye by living cells gives a coloured formazan. Colour intensity is proportional to the number of growing cells, so it measures drug effect on proliferation.

cards.front: What are the limits of in vitro studies, according to the owner's text?
cards.back: No systemic effect can be studied, there is no in vivo dose-response, organ specificity is lacking, and chronic effects cannot be studied.

cards.front: Short note: Organ-on-a-chip and in silico models in drug evaluation

points: Models complex physiology more accurately than current cell-based assays
Experiment performed by computer simulation
Already used to predict genotoxicity of chemicals
Cell-based and chip models cannot show whole-body systemic effects
Computer hits must be confirmed in the laboratory: in one docking study about half the predicted molecules were active

cards.front: What is an in silico experiment?
cards.back: An experiment performed on a computer or by computer simulation of a biological system, used to speed drug discovery and reduce lab work.

cards.front: Short note: In vitro screening for drug interactions

points: Isolated human or animal liver microsomes are incubated with the drug of interest
Used to study metabolism and inhibition by other drugs
Intestinal permeability studies are also run in vitro
Competitive inhibition of a CYP isoenzyme raises levels of drugs it metabolises
Enzyme inducers speed up metabolism, lowering levels of co-administered drugs

cards.front: Why is an enzyme-inhibiting drug a drug-interaction risk?
cards.back: Competitive inhibition of a cytochrome P450 isoenzyme slows metabolism of co-administered drugs, raising their plasma levels. In vitro microsome tests can screen for this before clinical use.

cards.front: Short note: Flame photometry in pharmacological assays

points: Measures sodium, potassium and similar ions
In the Langendorff heart it estimates potassium in the coronary outflow
Potassium outflow correlates with the positive inotropic effect of cardiac glycosides

cards.front: Essay: Screening of a potential anti-diabetic agent

points: Diabetes models are chosen by the type of diabetes they copy
Type I and type II models differ in how hyperglycaemia is produced
Alloxan and streptozotocin (STZ) destroy beta cells; both produce DNA damage through free radicals or alkylation
STZ in adult rats (about 40 mg/kg IV): animals with blood glucose above 200 to 300 mg% are selected
Neonatal STZ: single dose to 1 to 5 day old pups gives impaired glucose tolerance and hyperglycaemia
Nicotinamide plus STZ and low-dose STZ with high-fat diet also give a type II-like state
Obese or diabetic strains: ob/ob mouse, KK mouse, NSY mouse, OLETF rat
Pancreatectomy of 70 to 90% of the gland produces hyperglycaemia
Alpha-glucosidase and sucrase inhibition (carbohydrate digestion)
Insulin secretion from beta cell lines; glucose uptake in muscle and adipocytes
Blood glucose estimated at intervals before and after the test substance
Chemical models give type I diabetes only, so a type II model is needed separately
Start with a rapid model, confirm in a type II model, then test mechanism in vitro

cards.front: Why does streptozotocin destroy pancreatic beta cells?
cards.back: STZ is taken up through the GLUT-2 transporter of beta cells. Its nitrosourea group alkylates DNA, and the resulting damage destroys the cells and produces hyperglycaemia.

cards.front: How is the neonatal STZ model of type II diabetes made?
cards.back: A single dose of STZ is given to 1-day-old pups (about 100 mg/kg i.p.), or about 120 mg/kg to 2 to 5-day-old pups. Beta cells then behave like those of type II patients.

cards.front: Short note: Experimental evaluation of anticonvulsant drugs

points: Maximal electroshock (MES): tonic flexion, tonic extension and clonic convulsions; tests tonic-clonic protection
Corneal electroshock with a seizure severity score; minimal electroshock threshold and extensor seizure latency
Pentylenetetrazol (PTZ) clonic seizures; strychnine, picrotoxin and bicuculline convulsions
Kindling: repeated electrical stimulation of the amygdala produces secondarily generalised seizures
GAERS and WAG/Rij rats (absence), audiogenic-seizure mice, GEPR rats: spontaneous seizures
Ethosuximide suppresses PTZ clonic seizures without changing MES; carbamazepine raises threshold to both

cards.front: Short note: Methods to produce convulsions in rats and mice

points: Brief high-intensity shock to the head or corneal electroshock of a rodent
PTZ, strychnine, picrotoxin and bicuculline (bicuculline is used in focal seizure tests)
Pilocarpine: status epilepticus at about 380 to 400 mg/kg i.p. in rats; lithium pre-treatment lowers the dose
Repeated stimulation of the hippocampal perforant path or amygdala leads to partial seizures that generalise
Spontaneous seizures in strains such as GAERS and audiogenic-seizure mice

cards.front: Which seizure does the maximal electroshock test produce and what is recorded?
cards.back: Tonic flexion, tonic extension and clonic convulsions after a brief high-intensity shock to the head. The test checks protection against tonic-clonic (generalised) seizures.

cards.front: What does pentylenetetrazol produce in rodents?
cards.back: Clonic seizures. Ethosuximide suppresses PTZ clonic seizures at doses that produce no other discernible effect.

cards.front: What is the kindling model?
cards.back: Repeated electrical stimulation of a limbic site (e.g. amygdala) gradually produces seizures that become secondarily generalised, mimicking human focal epilepsy.

cards.front: Short note: Experimental evaluation of an antihypertensive drug

points: Spontaneously hypertensive rat (SHR) and related strains
Drug- or hormone-induced: cholinomimetic (physostigmine, oxotremorine), angiotensin II infusion, cadmium, chronic L-NAME
Transgenic rats overexpressing renin (TGR)
Tail-cuff pressure and heart rate in conscious rats
Invasive arterial pressure in anaesthetised animals (cat, rat) with autonomic drugs
Rabbit aorta rings: KCl contraction, relaxation by calcium antagonists
Langendorff heart: coronary flow and contractility

cards.front: Essay: Methods for the evaluation of antihypertensive drugs

points: Antihypertensives are judged by lowering arterial pressure in animals with hypertension
SHR: hypertension with complications; SHRSP, obese SHR
Wistar fatty rats: hypertension with hyperinsulinaemia
Induced: cholinomimetic (central then sympathetic), angiotensin II over 4 to 8 weeks, cadmium, chronic nitric oxide inhibition
Transgenic renin rats (TGR mREN2) model local renin-angiotensin activity
Non-invasive tail-cuff method in conscious rats
Direct arterial pressure under anaesthesia for accuracy
Rabbit aorta: calcium antagonism tested by relaxation after KCl
Langendorff and isolated heart-lung preparations: coronary and cardiac effects
Models may not match essential hypertension (e.g. renal sodium handling in the Milan strain)
Drug-induced models show mechanism but are artificial

cards.front: What is the spontaneously hypertensive rat (SHR)?
cards.back: A rat strain that develops moderate to severe hypertension and complications of hypertension without any drug. It is the standard genetic model of hypertension.

cards.front: What is the non-invasive tail-cuff method of blood pressure measurement?
cards.back: A cuff on the tail measures arterial pressure and heart rate in a conscious, restrained rat. It is sensitive and avoids surgery.

cards.front: Cholinomimetic-induced hypertension: how is it mediated?
cards.back: Physostigmine and oxotremorine raise blood pressure through central cholinergic activation, with a peripheral sympathetic component. Pre-treatment with methylscopolamine blocks the initial fall.

cards.front: Short note: Cardiovascular drug development: challenges and non-invasive evaluation

points: Models of acute heart failure are first induced (e.g. barbiturate overdose) before a positive inotrope can be judged
Some hypertension models need weeks to develop (angiotensin II 4 to 8 weeks)
Arrhythmia models cover WPW, atrial flutter, atrial and ventricular fibrillation
Tail-cuff pressure and heart rate in conscious rats
Isolated heart preparations recording rate, force and coronary flow without surgery on the animal
Only the animal methods are grounded in the owner's books; human non-invasive methods are not stated in them

cards.front: What does a Langendorff heart preparation measure?
cards.back: Heart rate by chronometer, contractile force by a force transducer, coronary flow, left ventricular pressure with dp/dt max, and oxygen consumption in the isolated perfused heart.

cards.front: Which animal arrhythmia model is used for anti-arrhythmic screening?
cards.back: Animal models include Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation and ventricular fibrillation, each used to test anti-arrhythmic drugs.

cards.front: Short note: Screening for anti-ulcer activity

points: Rats fasted 48 hours, pylorus tied under ether; drug given for two days before
Killed 19 hours later; gastric pH, free and total acidity measured
Ulcers graded 0 to 5 by size and severity; ulcer index calculated
Rats fasted 36 to 40 hours, restrained on a wire screen for 24 hours; forced swimming in a glass cylinder
Aspirin, phenylbutazone, indomethacin, ibuprofen by gavage; reserpine by injection
Histamine given to guinea pigs (with antihistamine protection of the animal); stomach examined and ulcers graded
Continuous recording of gastric acid in anaesthetised rat by pH change with a perfused NaOH solution; histamine or carbachol as secretagogue

cards.front: Essay: Screening of a new compound for anti-ulcer activity

points: Ulcers are produced in animals by pylorus ligation, stress, drugs or histamine
Protection (cytoprotection) and secretion (antisecretory) are tested separately
Shay rat pylorus ligation: fasted rats, ligation, sacrifice after 19 hours, ulcers graded 0 to 5
Restraint and forced-swim stress ulcers
Aspirin, phenylbutazone, indomethacin or ibuprofen as ulcerogenic agents; test drug given beforehand
Continuous gastric acid recording in anaesthetised rat with several doses
Guinea pig histamine-induced ulcer: drug tested against histamine
Isolated rat gastric fundus strip for direct contractile effects
Compare ulcer index and acidity with controls and a standard drug
Confirm in a second model before preclinical toxicity

cards.front: What is the Shay rat model?
cards.back: Pyloric ligation in fasted rats. Under light anaesthesia the pylorus is tied, drugs are given beforehand, and the stomach is examined 19 hours later for acidity and ulcers.

cards.front: How are gastric ulcers graded in the pylorus ligation model?
cards.back: Zero to five, depending on the size and severity of the ulcers (Barrett's grading). An ulcer index is then calculated from these grades.

cards.front: Name the agents used to produce ulcers in rats.
cards.back: Aspirin, phenylbutazone, indomethacin and ibuprofen (given by gavage), and reserpine (injected).

cards.front: What is the advantage of continuous gastric acid recording in one rat?
cards.back: Several doses of drug can be given to the same animal, and each inhibition or potentiation of the secretagogue response is recorded as a change in pH.

cards.front: Short note: Screening a new molecule for effect on intestinal motility

points: Charcoal meal in mice: drug 45 minutes before; charcoal travel as percentage of small intestine length
Castor oil in mice: copious (++), mild (+) or none (0) scored; activity score counts double for ++
Castor oil in rats: intraluminal fluid volume between pylorus and caecum after drug
Mouse defaecation: faeces counted over 4 hours; percentage reduction against control
Isolated guinea pig ileum or rabbit duodenum for direct effects of drug on contraction

cards.front: Charcoal meal test: what is the endpoint?
cards.back: Distance travelled by the charcoal meal along the small intestine, expressed as a percentage of total small-intestine length, 15 minutes after gavage.

cards.front: Castor oil test: what is scored in mice and in rats?
cards.back: In mice, diarrhoea is scored as copious, mild or none. In rats, the intraluminal fluid volume between the pylorus and caecum is measured.

cards.front: Short note: Screening for an antipsychotic drug

points: Catalepsy in rodents: a drug-induced posture is maintained; typical antipsychotics produce it
Foot-shock induced aggression in mice; artificial hibernation in rats; influence on behaviour of cotton rats
Catalepsy correlates with extrapyramidal side effects, which are mediated by dopamine blockade
Phenothiazine and butyrophenone neuroleptics block D2 receptors and, to some extent, D1 receptors
A valid model should show antipsychotic activity and predict clinical efficacy

cards.front: What is catalepsy in a rodent test, and what does it predict?
cards.back: A drug-induced failure to move out of an imposed posture. It predicts extrapyramidal side effects, which come from dopamine blockade.

cards.front: Which receptor do typical antipsychotics block?
cards.back: Mainly dopamine D2 receptors, with some alpha-adrenergic blockade for phenothiazines and butyrophenones.

cards.front: Short note: Experimental evaluation of an antidepressant

points: Forced swim test and tail suspension test in mice: immobility time reduced by antidepressants
Learned helplessness in rats (originally inescapable shock in dogs)
Chronic mild stress: uncontrollable mild stressors over days
Reserpine-induced hypothermia; amphetamine and norepinephrine potentiation; tetrabenazine antagonism; 5-HTP potentiation; yohimbine toxicity
Inhibition of tritiated noradrenaline, dopamine or serotonin uptake in brain synaptosomes
Binding to monoamine transporters
Effect is judged by suppression or reduction of immobility time, with statistics

cards.front: What is the forced swim test and how is an antidepressant read from it?
cards.back: Rodents placed in water become immobile. An antidepressant reduces the immobility time compared with control.

cards.front: What is learned helplessness as a depression model?
cards.back: Animals exposed to inescapable stress fail to escape later, a behavioural state used to simulate depression. It was first described in dogs and later used in rats and mice.

cards.front: Why test a candidate antidepressant in an amine uptake assay?
cards.back: It shows whether the drug blocks noradrenaline, dopamine or serotonin uptake into synaptosomes, linking the behavioural result to a mechanism.

cards.front: Short note: Bioassay methods for analgesics

points: Hot plate at 55 C: reaction time (lick of paw) with cut-off of 30 seconds
Tail-flick under radiant heat; tail-immersion at 55 C
Writhing test: phenylquinone or acetic acid i.p. in mice; 4% NaCl writhing in rats (said to predict analgesia in man)
Tail clip in mice (pressure) and other pain-state models with mechanical or electrical stimuli
Discoordination test on a rotating drum to exclude sedation or muscle relaxation
Naloxone antagonism (pA2) with different tests

cards.front: Hot-plate test: what is the endpoint?
cards.back: Reaction time for the mouse or rat to lick its fore or hind paws on a plate kept at 55 C. A cut-off of 30 seconds protects the paws.

cards.front: Tail-flick test: what is the endpoint?
cards.back: The time the animal takes to withdraw its tail from a radiant heat source, with pre-selection of animals whose baseline times are consistent.

cards.front: Why run a discoordination test with analgesic screening?
cards.back: Animals placed on a slowly rotating wire-mesh drum that fall off are excluded. Sedatives and muscle relaxants can give false positive analgesic results.

cards.front: Short note: Instruments used to evaluate CNS depressants in animals

points: Rota-rod: fore and hind limb coordination on a rotating rod
Horizontal bar, static rods and parallel bars; chimney test
Traction (grip strength) test on a horizontal wire: animal must grip and climb within 5 seconds
Inclined plane for muscle relaxants
Righting reflex loss: CNS depressants cause loss of righting in animals at a dose
Mouse climbs back out of a glass tube; failure within 30 seconds means relaxed muscles

cards.front: What does the rota-rod test measure?
cards.back: Motor coordination of the fore and hind limbs. Drugs that impair coordination make the animal fall from the rotating rod sooner.

cards.front: Why is loss of the righting reflex used to judge CNS depressants?
cards.back: Almost all CNS depressant drugs cause loss of the righting reflex at a certain dose, so it is an ideal simple measure of depression.

cards.front: Short note: Experimental evaluation of diuretic agents

points: Saluretic, natriuretic and carbonic anhydrase inhibitory effects tested in healthy volunteers
Potassium-sparing diuretics act on distal tubule and collecting duct and give a mild saluretic effect
Thiazides act on the cortical diluting segment
Some diuretics first dilate veins, reducing filling pressure, before any saluretic effect appears
Preclinical rodent diuretic screening methods are not stated in the owner books

cards.front: Where do potassium-sparing diuretics act?
cards.back: In the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. They produce only a mild saluretic effect.

cards.front: Why can a diuretic relieve congestion before its saluretic action?
cards.back: Venodilator action increases venous capacitance and lowers ventricular filling pressure first. This is prostaglandin mediated and precedes the saluretic response.

cards.front: Short note: Screening for anti-fertility activity

points: Demonstrate temporary, fully reversible sterility in laboratory animals
Rats are commonly used; mice, rabbits and monkeys also possible
Cohabitation test: vaginal smear for seven days; pairing; pregnancy and litter counts
Unilateral ovariectomy: ovarian weight fall means ovulation inhibition
Uterine weight changes (oestrogenic); deciduoma (progestational)
Implants, resorptions, histology
Cohabitation with two known-fertile females; sperm from the epididymis
Testing over 12 weeks covers the 9-week spermatogenic cycle; oligospermia or aspermia shows suppression
Anti-ovulatory, oestrogenic, anti-gonadotrophic, progestational, anti-progestational, pre-implantation tests

cards.front: What does a fall in ovarian weight after unilateral ovariectomy indicate?
cards.back: Inhibition of ovulation through suppressed follicle-stimulating hormone, so the treated ovary weight is lower than the control.

cards.front: What does a deciduoma test show?
cards.back: Development of a deciduoma in the uterus indicates progestational action.

cards.front: Short note: Screening for an antimalarial agent

points: Artemisinin resistance (delayed parasite clearance) and mutations that confer resistance are already reported
Combination with longer-acting partner drugs protects against selection of artemisinin resistance
Preclinical antimalarial screening methods (e.g. in vivo rodent malaria tests) are not in the owner books

cards.front: Why is combination therapy used in malaria?
cards.back: Combinations with longer-acting partner drugs protect the artemisinin component from selection of resistant parasites.

cards.front: Short note: Zebrafish as an experimental model

points: Vertebrate with a backbone, so closer to humans than fruit fly or worm models
Embryo develops into a newly formed fish in 2 to 4 days and can be watched under a microscope
Kept at high density in small tanks, so cheaper than many laboratory animals
Lifespan about 5 years; adult length about 6 cm
Studies of embryo development and genetics

cards.front: Why are zebrafish embryos useful for drug testing?
cards.back: They develop into a fish within 2 to 4 days and can be observed under a microscope, allowing early developmental effects to be seen.

cards.front: Short note: The laboratory rat as an experimental animal

points: Randomly bred strains from the Norway rat; Wistar and Sprague Dawley preferred for handling, sensitivity and low cost
Albino (pink-eyed white) rat is the oldest purposely bred mutation
Nude rat: no normal thymus and no mature T cells; preferred in immunological research
Hypertensive strains such as the SHR and the Milan strain are used for hypertension research
Used for behaviour, pharmacology, physiology, neurosciences, immunogenetics, transplantation, cancer risk, cardiovascular disease and ageing
Development of inbred, congenic and recombinant strains widened their use

cards.front: Which two outbred rat strains are preferred and why?
cards.back: Wistar and Sprague Dawley: easy handling, sensitivity and low cost.

cards.front: What is a nude rat?
cards.back: A rat that lacks a normal thymus and mature T cells, is nearly hairless, and is preferred in immunological research.

cards.front: Short note: Guinea pig (Cavia porcellus) as an experimental animal

points: Introduced into Europe from South America about 400 years ago
Cannot make its own vitamin C, so ascorbic acid is added: 200 mg/L daily in chow-only diets, or 1 g/L weekly if fed greens
Newborns eat solid food by day 5 and are weaned by 2 weeks; oestrous cycle 13 to 20 days (average 16)
Isolated guinea pig ileum and trachea are standard bioassay tissues

cards.front: Why must guinea pigs be given vitamin C?
cards.back: Guinea pigs cannot synthesise vitamin C, so it must be added to their diet (200 mg/L daily on chow alone).

cards.front: Short note: Inbred strains of animals in experimentation

points: Produced by mating brother and sister or parent and offspring for at least 20 generations
Homozygous, so responses are consistent and reproducible
Less variable population reduces sampling error in bioassays
Homogeneous strains are unwise in toxicity testing, because unexpected effects appear in wider variability
Heterozygous outbred stock improves robustness
Inbred and mutant mice are the preferred models for identifying genes; genetic characterisation is needed

cards.front: What is an inbred strain?
cards.back: A strain produced by sibling or parent-offspring mating for at least 20 generations, so its animals are homozygous and genetically uniform.

cards.front: Short note: Transgenic animals

points: Prepare a gene construct; introduce it by DNA microinjection, embryonic stem cell mediated transfer, or retrovirus
Germ-line chimeras are bred until homozygous transgenic animals are obtained
Mutant allele put into ES cells by homologous recombination; chimeras mated to get homozygous knockouts
Knockout mice model inherited human disease and test treatments
Knock-in of human immunoglobulin genes gives humanised antibodies
Stem-cell gene correction is a foreseen clinical use
Ethical and welfare issues apply to transgenic animal use

cards.front: What are the main methods of making a transgenic animal?
cards.back: DNA microinjection, embryonic stem cell mediated gene transfer and retrovirus-mediated gene transfer.

cards.front: Describe the steps to produce a gene-knockout mouse.
cards.back: Mutant allele introduced into ES cells by homologous recombination; these cells go into early embryos to form chimeras; chimeras are mated to get germ-line heterozygotes; heterozygotes are mated to get homozygous knockouts.

cards.front: Short note: Toxicity testing of a new drug in animals

points: Single dose; LD50 in a rodent and a non-rodent by two routes
Signs recorded: tremors, convulsions, ataxia, sedation, respiratory depression
Daily doses for about two to three weeks in rats, with body weight and blood measurements
Daily doses for six months in rat and dog; renal and hepatic function, haematology and histology
Effects on fertility and teratogenic potential if the drug will be used in women of childbearing age

cards.front: Why are two species used in toxicity studies?
cards.back: Species differ in their response to toxins. A toxic effect seen in both rat and dog probably involves a common mechanism that is likely in man; an effect in only one species is less likely to occur in man.

cards.front: What is the purpose of the LD50 in acute toxicity?
cards.back: It finds the single dose that kills 50% of a species, for a 24-hour test with one rodent and one non-rodent by two routes.

cards.front: How is a first human dose estimated from animal toxicity?
cards.back: Take the minimum effective dose from the animal data. If the rat was tested, use one two-hundredth of it; if the dog was tested, use one tenth. Surface-area conversion gives a wider margin.

cards.front: Short note: Safety factor and first-in-human dose

points: No observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) in the most sensitive animal species
Convert to human equivalent dose (HED) by body surface area
Divide HED by a default safety factor of 10 for the maximum recommended starting dose
Dose escalation is slow; first doses are well below the NOAEL

cards.front: What is the no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL)?
cards.back: The highest dose in animal studies at which no adverse effect is seen. It is the starting point for estimating the first human dose.

cards.front: What safety factor is applied to the human equivalent dose?
cards.back: A default safety factor of 10 is divided into the HED to give the maximum recommended starting dose.

cards.front: Short note: Genotoxicity testing

points: Detect mutagenic and carcinogenic potential, since gene mutation can cause carcinogenesis
Bacterial reverse mutation (Ames) test in two or three bacteria; mammalian cells for gene mutation, clastogenicity, aneuploidy
Dose-dependent in vivo tests on a case-by-case basis; transgenic animals are more appropriate
Mammalian bone marrow cells for somatic mutation
Spontaneous reversions occur in each strain; the choice of extra test depends on chemical structure

cards.front: What is the principle of the Ames test?
cards.back: Histidine-dependent Salmonella typhimurium and E. coli strains can grow only if a mutation reverts. Mutagenic compounds increase revertant colonies above the spontaneous background.

cards.front: Short note: Neurotoxicity screening of a new drug

points: Histopathological and behavioural neurotoxicity in adult rodents
Dosing for 28 days or more than 90 days; memory, sensory and learning changes evaluated
In vitro neurotoxicity testing recommended by regulators since 1998
Systems: neural cell lines, organotypic explants, re-aggregating cultures
Rodent neurotoxicity relies on histology and behaviour, so subtle effects may be missed

cards.front: Short note: Developmental neurotoxicity testing

points: Non-mammalian species with conserved neurodevelopmental process
In vitro cell culture models
In silico models
Cell proliferation, migration, differentiation, survival and apoptosis
Synaptogenesis, myelination, axonal and dendritic outgrowth
Chick embryo, wild-type and transgenic rodents, human neural progenitor cells
In vitro: small quantity, controlled and quick, but no systemic effect and no in vivo dose-response

cards.front: Name three in vitro sources of tissue for developmental neurotoxicity models.
cards.back: Chick embryos, rat and mouse (wild type or transgenic) tissue, and human neural progenitor cells from aborted foetuses or stem cell lines.

cards.front: Short note: Regulatory toxicity studies required for a new drug

points: Genetic toxicity testing and carcinogenicity testing
Embryotoxicity and developmental toxicity; one-generation and two-generation reproduction studies
Neurotoxicity studies in rodents; local toxicity
Acute inhalation, topical, skin sensitisation, photo-allergy and dermal photo-toxicity; vaginal and rectal tolerance
Animal pharmacology and animal toxicology are required parts of the IND and NDA

cards.front: What is the purpose of a subacute toxicity study?
cards.back: Daily dosing for a shorter period (about two to three weeks in rats) to find organ, body weight and haematology changes before a long-term study.

cards.front: Short note: Biomarkers in clinical and preclinical evaluation

points: Biomarkers help discover the mechanism and pathway of disease and the response to treatment
Biomarker data are added to studies by therapeutic area
Serum enzyme levels such as liver enzymes serve as surrogate markers of toxicity
Overt toxicity and exaggerated pharmacodynamic effects are used with them to set the NOAEL
Translational medicine links animal and human biomarker data

cards.front: Give an example of a surrogate marker of drug toxicity.
cards.back: Serum liver enzyme levels, which signal hepatocellular damage.

cards.front: Short note: Regulatory aspects of biopharmaceuticals

points: Generics: small, well-defined molecules; bioequivalence studies in healthy volunteers
Biosimilars: large, complex and variable molecules; large clinical trials in patients
Biosimilar manufacturing needs more quality tests and is sensitive to production change
WHO Expert Committee on Biological Standardisation has guidelines for biotherapeutic similarity
IND and NDA include animal pharmacology and toxicology, clinical data and prescribing information

cards.front: How do biosimilar approval requirements differ from generics?
cards.back: Generics need bioequivalence studies in healthy volunteers. Biosimilars need large clinical trials in patients, because the molecules are complex and cannot be fully characterised.

cards.front: What does the owner's text say about drug dependence risk in CNS drugs?
cards.back: Recreational use of some CNS-acting drugs can lead to physical dependence, with large societal impact.

cards.front: Why is post-marketing surveillance needed after accelerated approval?
cards.back: Post-marketing trials are required to validate the anticipated clinical benefit that was accepted on accelerated approval.

cards.front: Short note: Animal experimentation in new drug development: aim, utility and limits

points: Predict efficacy and toxicity before first human exposure
Pharmacological profile tested in animals at each step of development
Screening, mechanism, pharmacokinetics and toxicity studies in two species
Lead optimisation, preclinical development and IND filing follow the animal data
Species differ; an effect in one species does not guarantee the human effect
Inbred strains give less variation but may hide unexpected effects
Man is a distinct species, so safe animal dose is not always safe in man

cards.front: Short note: Obesity models in experimental animals

points: High-fat diet fed to rats, with or without low-dose STZ, gives a metabolic state like type 2 diabetes
Ob/ob mouse and Zucker-derived Wistar fatty rats; hyperinsulinaemia develops after 16 weeks in the fatty rat
Diet and genetic models differ in the cause of obesity

cards.front: What is pA2 for a competitive antagonist?
cards.back: The negative log molar concentration of antagonist that doubles the agonist's EC50, i.e. the dose ratio is 2 (log(DR minus 1) = 0). It is read from a Schild plot.

cards.front: Short note: Preclinical and clinical evaluation of a new anticonvulsant

points: Electroshock (MES) and chemical (PTZ) tests in rodents for activity
Genetic and kindling models to check efficacy against epilepsy types
Confirm with motor-impairment tests (rota-rod) to check side effects
Acute, subacute and chronic toxicity in a rodent and a non-rodent
First human dose from the NOAEL with a safety factor of 10
After the IND is filed, human studies proceed through clinical trial phases
Animal findings guide the human dose and monitoring

cards.front: Short note: In silico models in drug design: types, advantages and disadvantages

points: Experiments performed on computer or by simulation of biological systems
Analysis of biological and medical data from many sources by software
Protein-ligand docking to screen candidate molecules
Models of cellular behaviour and of disease (e.g. an in silico tuberculosis model)
Prediction of genotoxicity of chemicals
Speeds up discovery and reduces the need for costly laboratory work and trials
Can be used before any animal or human exposure
Hits must be confirmed in the laboratory: about half the molecules in one docking study were active
Depends on the quality of the underlying model and data

cards.front: Give one example of an in silico docking study mentioned in the owner's text.
cards.back: Protein-ligand docking (EADock) found potential inhibitors of a cancer-associated enzyme; about half the predicted molecules were later shown active in the laboratory.

cards.front: What do changes in uterine weight and a deciduoma indicate?
cards.back: Changes in uterine weight point to oestrogenic or anti-oestrogenic action; a deciduoma points to progestational action.

cards.front: What is an anti-ovulatory test in female rats?
cards.back: Checking whether a drug stops ovulation, e.g. by vaginal smear for normal oestrous cycle, and by ovarian weight and histology after unilateral ovariectomy.

cards.front: Cell-line cytotoxicity test: what is measured?
cards.back: Growth of actively dividing mammalian cells in microplate wells, with and without the test material; colour intensity tracks cell number.

cards.front: Why run a normal cell line beside cancer cell lines?
cards.back: To judge selectivity: whether the material hits cancer cells more than normal cells.

cards.front: MTT and XTT assays: what is the principle?
cards.back: Mitochondria of viable cells reduce the dye to a coloured formazan read on a plate reader. XTT formazan dissolves in water; MTT needs a solubilising step.

cards.front: What is IC50 in cell-line toxicity?
cards.back: The concentration of material that inhibits a biological or biochemical function by 50 per cent; found by cell counts or cytotoxicity readings.

cards.front: How does trypan blue exclusion count living cells?
cards.back: The dye enters only dead cells, so the unstained cells counted on a haemocytometer are viable.

cards.front: Which tests tell apoptosis from necrosis in cell lines?
cards.back: Fluorescence microscopy (acridine orange and ethidium bromide), confocal imaging with nuclear dyes, DNA fragmentation on agarose gel, and annexin V/propidium iodide flow cytometry.

cards.front: Short note: In vitro cell-line toxicity testing

points: Cultured, actively dividing mammalian cells in microplates
Growth with versus without the test material
MTT or XTT reduction to formazan
Trypan blue exclusion counts; IC50 from cell counts or cytotoxicity
Selectivity from a normal cell line
Apoptosis vs necrosis: microscopy, DNA laddering, flow cytometry
Cell-cycle arrest by flow cytometry
Many materials screened fast, tiny quantities
Costly equipment, aseptic work, poor for insoluble materials

cards.front: Name two drawbacks of cell-line toxicity assays.
cards.back: Costly, sophisticated equipment under aseptic conditions; unreliable results for water-insoluble materials unless they dissolve in under 1 per cent DMSO.

cards.front: 2 x 2 factorial design: which four groups?
cards.back: A alone, B alone, A plus B, and neither (placebo), with subjects randomly allocated to one group.

cards.front: Why use a factorial design?
cards.back: It tests two treatments with the same subjects, examines their interaction, and maps the dose-response of the combination.

cards.front: Short note: Factorial design in experiments

points: Factors each set at levels, e.g. 2 x 2 or 2 x 3
Subjects randomly allocated to each combination
Factorial ANOVA: effect of each factor
Whether the factors act independently or depend on each other
Efficient use of subjects
Detects interaction between treatments

cards.front: Short note: Acute toxicity studies in animals

points: Effect of a single dose in a species
Standard testing: one rodent and one non-rodent species, at least two routes, one of them the proposed human route
Fixed dose procedure (non-lethal endpoint)
Acute toxic category method (sequential, three animals per step)
Up-and-down procedure (staircase, one animal at 48 h intervals)
LD50 introduced by Trevan (1920)
Draize method for eye and skin irritation in rabbits
Lethal endpoint and animal numbers in classical designs
Single-dose data do not cover repeated-dose toxicity

cards.front: Essay: Acute toxicity studies on animals: aims, methodology and limitations

points: Acute toxicity = effects of one dose in a species
LD50 history and its place in drug development
Identify target organs and dose range
Guide the starting dose for later studies
Two species (rodent and non-rodent), two routes
Fixed dose procedure at 5, 50, 500 and 2000 mg/kg
Acute toxic category method: three animals of one sex per step
Up-and-down procedure: one animal, 48 h intervals, female rodents
Classical LD50 is lethal and uses many animals
Acute data do not predict repeated-dose or chronic effects

cards.front: What is the fixed dose procedure for?
cards.back: Assessing non-lethal toxicity: fixed doses of 5, 50, 500 and 2000 mg/kg, with animals observed for a set period.

cards.front: Up-and-down procedure: how is it run?
cards.back: One animal at a time is dosed sequentially at 48 h intervals (staircase design); it is preferred because it cuts animal numbers.

cards.front: Carcinogenicity study: when is it ended?
cards.back: If no tumours appear, it ends after about 18 months in mice and hamsters and 24 months in rats.

cards.front: Embryotoxicity study: when is the drug given and when is the foetus examined?
cards.back: Dosed from day 8 to 14 of pregnancy; caesarean section on day 21 to examine foetuses.

cards.front: Short note: Genotoxicity studies on animals

points: Detect gene mutations, chromosome changes and DNA sequence alteration
Mutations can lead to carcinogenesis, so mutagenicity is checked in drug development
In vitro: two or three bacterial and mammalian cell tests
Rodent chromosome assay and dominant lethal assay in whole animals
Systems are bacteria, cells and rodents, so the results need interpretation in humans
Chromosomal findings depend on the test system

cards.front: Short note: Specialised toxicity studies and regulatory requirement

points: Rodents and non-rodents, over most of the lifespan
Ended after about 18 months (mice, hamsters) or 24 months (rats) if no tumours
One-generation study: dosing for a spermatogenic cycle (males) and two oestrous cycles (females)
Two-generation study: parental mating and offspring assessment
Dosing days 8 to 14 of pregnancy
Caesarean section on day 21
Rodent behaviour, histopathology and neurological function

cards.front: Apomorphine emesis model: which species and dose?
cards.back: Dogs given apomorphine 0.15 mg/kg vomit; a test drug is judged by how much it reduces the emesis.

cards.front: Why do dopamine blockers reduce apomorphine emesis?
cards.back: Apomorphine acts on dopamine receptors; neuroleptics that block dopamine (e.g. metoclopramide) relieve the emetic response.

cards.front: Short note: Screening for anti-emetic activity

points: Apomorphine stimulates dopamine receptors and causes emesis in dogs
Give apomorphine with the test drug or vehicle
Score the emetic response against control
Dopamine-blocking drugs (metoclopramide) reduce emesis
Anti-emetic activity is inferred from reduced emesis
